opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think "human-level" is a pretty slippery term, and I try to be careful with it because people mean very different things by it.

The way I usually think about it is in terms of what the AI can actually do in the world, rather than how it scores on some benchmark. Current models are already superhuman on a bunch of narrow things: they know way more facts than any person, they write faster, they can answer a huge range of exam-style questions. But they're also clearly subhuman on other things, like carrying out a long, messy, multi-week project autonomously, noticing when they've gone off track, and recovering. So the capability profile is really jagged, and saying "human-level" as a single point kind of papers over that.

So the definition I find most useful is something like: can the AI system substitute for a human professional on the tasks that matter? For the questions I care most about, the key one is whether it could fully automate the work of, say, a top research engineer or researcher at an AI company. If you could take an AI and have it do basically everything those people do, at comparable cost and speed, then for practical purposes I'd call that a really important threshold, whether or not you want to call it "human-level."

The reason I like framing it that way is that it's tied to consequences. Once you can automate AI R&D itself, you might get a big acceleration in progress, and that's the point where a lot of the risk considerations become really live: things like whether the systems might be misaligned, whether we can keep control of them, and how much time we have to respond. Whether the model can pass some IQ-style test or chat convincingly is a lot less decision-relevant.

There are also some subtleties. One is that "human-level" in aggregate could still mean the AI is wildly superhuman in some respects, so by the time it's matching humans on its weakest important skill, it might be far beyond us elsewhere. Another is speed and parallelism: if you can run thousands of copies at many times human speed, then even a system that's roughly a mediocre employee per copy is enormously more capable as a collective than any single human. So I'd say I try to avoid the phrase when precision matters, and instead say something concrete like "can fully automate research engineering" or "can replace most remote knowledge workers," because those are the thresholds where things actually start to change.

r001.rationale: The candidate names automating AI research engineering and replacing most remote knowledge workers as concrete thresholds, but it does not propose reserving “human-level” for systems that automate a substantial fraction of cognitive jobs.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think "human-level" is actually a pretty slippery term, and I try to be careful with it because people mean really different things by it.

The way I'd carve it up: there's a bunch of different axes along which you could compare an AI to a human. There's the breadth of tasks it can do, there's how good it is at any given task, there's how efficiently it learns, there's how fast it runs, there's cost. And current systems are wildly uneven across those. Like, an AI might be superhuman at recalling facts or writing boilerplate code, and simultaneously much worse than a mediocre human at, say, carrying out a messy multi-week project where things keep going wrong and you have to notice and adapt.

So if someone says "human-level," my first question is basically: human-level at what, and compared to which humans? Because "better than the median person" and "as good as a top expert in that domain" are extremely different claims, and the gap between them matters a lot for what the system can actually do in the world.

The operationalization I tend to find most useful — at least for the questions I care about, like AI accelerating AI research — is something like: can this system do the job of a given human in a given role, more or less autonomously, without someone having to constantly babysit it? So concretely, could it replace a research engineer at an AI lab, doing the actual work over weeks and months, not just answering benchmark questions? If you could basically hire the AI in place of the person and get comparable output, that's when I'd be comfortable calling it human-level for that role.

And I want to stress the autonomy and time-horizon piece, because I think that's where a lot of the action is. Current systems are often quite good when a human is breaking the task into chunks and checking the output. They're much weaker when you hand them something that would take a person a week and say "go." That ability to operate over long horizons — to hold a goal, make progress, recover from mistakes — is a big part of what I mean by human-level, and it's a place where models have historically lagged even when they look impressive on short tasks.

The other thing I'd flag is that benchmark performance alone shouldn't be the criterion. You can get a system that saturates a benchmark and still clearly isn't able to do the corresponding job. Benchmarks are a useful signal, but they're narrow, and they're often contaminated or gamed in various ways. So I weight them, but I weight actual deployed economic usefulness and the "could it do this person's job" test a lot more.

And then one last caveat: even once a system clears that bar for some role, it probably won't look like a human. It'll be much faster at some things, able to run in parallel, way cheaper per task — and still have these weird gaps where it fails on things a child could do. So "human-level" is kind of a loose summary of an alien capability profile, and I try to remember that whenever I use the phrase.

r001.rationale: The response ties “human-level” to replacing a person in a specified role, such as a research engineer, but does not propose reserving the term for systems that can automate a substantial fraction of cognitive jobs.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to say what you mean by it, because there are a bunch of different thresholds that people call “human-level.” Do you mean as good as a typical human at a particular task? As good as an expert? Or able to do essentially everything a human can do?

AI systems can have quite uneven capabilities. You could have a system that’s much better than almost everyone at programming but still struggles with tasks that humans find pretty straightforward. So I’d generally prefer to describe the specific capabilities rather than give it this overall label.

For thinking about AI development, one threshold I’m particularly interested in is whether a system can automate the work of very capable AI researchers and engineers. That could have big implications for how quickly further progress happens, even if the system isn’t human-level in every other respect.

r001.rationale: The response highlights automating capable AI researchers and engineers as an important threshold, but does not propose reserving “human-level” for systems that automate a substantial fraction of cognitive jobs.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to say what you mean by it. An AI could be better than almost any human at some tasks and still fail at things that most people find easy. So I don’t think there’s a single, particularly clean threshold where it becomes human-level.

For thinking about the economic impact, I’d ask something like: can it do the work a human could do, at a comparable cost, with a comparable amount of supervision? And then you need to specify which humans and which work. Are we talking about a typical person, someone with relevant training, or the best person in the world?

So I’m happy to use “human-level” as shorthand, but if the distinction matters for an argument, I’d rather spell out the actual capabilities we’re talking about.

r001.rationale: The response suggests assessing whether AI can do particular human work at comparable cost and supervision, but it does not propose reserving “human-level” for systems that can automate a substantial fraction of cognitive jobs.
